screens.body:
A test plan is exactly what it sounds like: a plan for testing. What will we test? How? Who runs it? When? What's out of scope?

You don't need a 50-page document. Even a short list — "test signup, test payments, skip the admin panel for now" — beats testing randomly.

options: What, how, who, and when of testing
check.question: A test plan covers…

screens.heading: What is a test plan?
screens.keyPoint: A short plan beats random testing.

screens.body:
Coverage measures how much of your code your tests actually run — usually as a percentage. 80% coverage means tests execute 80% of your lines.

Coverage is a guide, not a guarantee. You can have 100% coverage and still miss the bug where two features interact badly. Aim high, but don't worship the number.

options: More of your code is exercised — but bugs can still hide
check.question: High coverage means…

screens.heading: Test coverage
screens.keyPoint: Coverage is a guide, not a guarantee.

screens.body:
Found a bug? It goes on a journey: reported → triaged (is it real? how bad?) → assigned → fixed → verified (does the fix work?) → closed.

Skipping "verified" is how fixed bugs come back from the dead. Always re-test the fix.

options: Verify the fix works, then close
check.question: After a bug is fixed, the next step is…

screens.heading: The bug lifecycle
screens.keyPoint: Fixed isn't done until the fix is verified.

screens.body:
A great bug report has: steps to reproduce, what you expected, what actually happened, and your environment (browser, OS).

"It doesn't work" helps nobody. "Clicking Pay twice charges me twice — expected one charge — Chrome on Windows" gets fixed by lunch.

check.question: The most important part of a bug report is…

screens.heading: Writing a bug report people can use
screens.keyPoint: Repro steps turn complaints into fixes.

screens.body:
Severity = how bad is the bug. Priority = how fast do we fix it. They're different!

A typo on the homepage: low severity (nothing breaks), high priority (everyone sees it). A rare crash in an old settings page: high severity, low priority. Mixing them up is how critical bugs wait in line behind typos.

options: How bad / how fast we fix
check.question: Severity is ___; priority is ___.

screens.heading: Severity vs priority
screens.keyPoint: Bad-ness and fix-speed are different axes.

screens.body:
You fix a bug or add a feature — and accidentally break something that used to work. Regression testing catches that: re-running old tests after every change.

This is where automated suites earn their keep. Humans get bored re-testing; scripts don't.

options: Re-runs old tests after changes to catch new breakage
check.question: Regression testing…

screens.heading: Regression testing
screens.keyPoint: Re-test the old stuff after every change.

screens.body:
Your birthday RSVP form added a dietary-needs field last week. Did the plus-one logic still work after? That's a regression question.

And Olamide's coconut note plus Megan's "Fish" — your caterer plan is basically a bug report with severity (allergy!) and priority (tell the caterer now).
screens.heading: Why this matters for you
screens.keyPoint: You already triage bugs in real life.
